item.text: {"text":"Recent work distinguishes explanation plausibility from evidence support. A [2026 recommendation study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2026.1827553/full) separates citation validity, semantic claim support, fabricated-history checks, and perceived usefulness: valid evidence IDs alone do not establish truth. A [2024 human study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02018) finds explanations can increase self-reported trust, reinforcing the need to calibrate judgments against evidence rather than persuasiveness. For this task, retain exact title/description spans and history-item IDs supporting each probe; distinguish observed metadata relationships from claims about user preferences or needs.\n\nSelective prediction provides a useful evaluation framework: measure coverage alongside error among answered cases, allowing explicit abstention when evidence is insufficient ([2024 study](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.208/)). Proposed adaptation: label direct relevance only with specific shared attributes; adjacent relevance with an explicit complementary relationship; compatibility conflict only with documented incompatible requirements. Treat similar recommendations as potential redundancy, not proof of ownership or dissatisfaction. Missing specifications should yield “insufficient information,” not compatibility or mismatch. Calibrate these rules through independent human annotation, adjudication, and agreement reporting; report supported-label precision and abstention by category and metadata completeness. These are design recommendations inferred from the literature, not validated Amazon compatibility labels. Histories and timestamps alone cannot establish unmet need, satisfaction, ownership, or simulator traits."}
